readings.title: How social media ceased to be social
body: 22 May 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Social media platforms used to be about communication between friends – now many are increasingly short video entertainment hubs. The business model is to increase the time people spend on their apps and increase ad revenue. But is there already a consumer backlash? Aurélia fixes herself a coffee, sits down in her beautiful garden not far from Paris and goes on Instagram "to relax." First up: "a guy I like a lot who does interior design. He's in Venice at the moment." She's into interior design, and has even just had two bird drawings by the 19th Century English designer William Morris tattooed on her arms. She scrolls down. Two kittens having a fight. "I love animals so I get a lot of animals. That's how it works, social media. You click on bananas and they give you bananas." There are ads too – although they look just like the other posts – for a robot-vacuum cleaner, a diet and bed linen (with Morris-inspired designs). But no friends. She has 198 on Instagram but she says "it's completely changed. I practically don’t see any friends' posts anymore." She’s pretty much given up posting herself. "I don't think anyone sees them anymore anyway."  While there remain committed social, amateur posters on Instagram and especially Facebook, the switch from communicating with people you know to scrolling through professionally made content from people you don't, is even more pronounced among young users. Kylian, 16, is in vocational training to become a chef. He's on TikTok and Youtube a lot, he says. "I like looking at videos more than photos or messages. I watch videos made by people I don't know. I don’t post at all. I'm a rather shy person. I stay in my bubble. I watch and that’s all. I keep my reactions to myself." "I spend a lot of time scrolling through videos made by content-creators," says Lucie, also 16. "They're more interesting than the posts of people I know." She doesn't post except sometimes "stories" which disappear after 24 hours.  Whether it's TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram, we are a long way from the "digital town square" of personal interaction that social media was even just a few years ago. In France, annual official Barometre du numerique 2026  shows 49% of social media users are "active only occasionally". In the UK, an Ofcom report   published in April showed a year-on-year drop of users who actively post from 61% to 49%. In the US, a Morning Consult survey of June last year found 28% reported posting less often than the previous year. Just 33% now post daily compared to 57% who use it for entertainment daily. The gap is a lot wider still for Gen Z – 18% active for 74% passive. Vanessa Lalo, a Paris-based clinical psychologist specialising in on-line behaviour, says "users have become more conscious that the traces you leave (on social media) stay there forever and some no longer want to maintain social media relations that can be superficial. Some don’t want the exposure to criticism that might be a risk when you post or the feeling that their post will seem poor alongside all the professional content". However, Lalo adds, people haven’t stopped posting, rather they are posting different things and in different places. "On TikTok, for example, young people publish a lot of content but it's more funny parodies and remixes of existing material. The goal is to make people laugh, not to tell people about their lives." That still happens, she says, but it’s moved from social media platforms like Instagram and Facebook to messaging sites like WhatsApp. There's also been a move towards private groups on Instagram and Snapchat. "These are much more intimate places where you're not bombarded with ads and content made by influencers," she says. "What we're seeing is social media splitting in two," says social media consultant Matt Navarra, author of the Geekout Newsletter. "Big platforms like Instagram and TikTok are becoming more about entertainment and discovery. WhatsApp is becoming the place people go to actually be social. The catch is, those kinds of spaces are harder for companies to make money from." Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business – Matt Navarra It was TikTok that helped to pioneer an algorithm that figures out from the moment you start scrolling what you like, and then fills your feed with material calculated to keep you on the app for the longest possible time. Now, says Matt Navarra, "Meta has built what it calls an AI system for unconnected content recommendations on Facebook and Instagram, which basically means, they're increasingly showing you stuff from people you don't follow because the machine thinks you're going to like it. It's not biased towards, is it a professional creator? Is it a brand? Is it a friend? If they can see that you've engaged with a friend a lot, you might see a lot more of their content. It's just that who you are friends with, who you follow, has become irrelevant in a way." This all means that small businesses, that have long used social media for free promotion have to up their game.   "There's a real opportunity for some small businesses," says Matt Navarra. "A bakery, florist, salon or local café can still break through if they have a good story, strong visuals or behind-the-scenes content people want to watch. But it also means the job has changed. Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business." The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow – Matt Navarra Social media is evolving into something passive like television, albeit television that adapts as you zap. Or rather which knows you so well that it doesn't seem to matter that much that it's taken the remote control. You give the platform information about yourself that it uses for commercial gain and, in return, it gives you content tailored to please you for free. The transition from truly social media to entertainment platform does seem to be paying off. "The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow," says Matt Navarra. Global social media ad revenue is expected to reach $317 billion (£236bn) in 2026, up from $277 billion (£206bn) last year. Meta is the biggest winner. Its ad sales already increased 22% year-on-year in 2025.  Ad sales are expected to hit $243 billion (£181bn) this year , enough to overtake Google for the first time. AI powered digital ad targeting is becoming ever more effective and precise. "The social platforms allow companies to put ads amongst the content that you're scrolling through. Every third or fourth scroll is an ad. And they are the world's best ad targeting engines. They know so much about your interests because of what you've looked at, liked, engaged with, what you've chosen to follow, the time you've spent in certain areas of the app, things like that," Navarra says.  "So advertisers will go in and say: 'I want to place an ad next to people in the UK who are between thirty and sixty years old and who are interested in DIY' and the social platforms will have that information and will place the ads accordingly." The price will depend on the number of impressions (clicks) the advertiser wants and how tight the criteria are. It costs more to place ads in the social media feeds of people who buy horses than people who buy ice-cream. More like this: •  TikTok is tracking you, even if you don't use the app. Here's how to stop it •  How to stop AI from turning your brain to mush •  This monkey selfie will protect you from AI slop Might there be a backlash coming? Don't many people go on to social media to see how friends are reacting to their posts or comments before settling down to scroll through professionally made content? Whether it's the shrinking social motivation to get on these apps or something else, the amount of time people spend on social media plateaued at an average of 141 minutes in 2025, down slightly from 143 minutes in 2024 . However, this is only part of the story, as the number of people using social media and the total time humanity spends on these apps continues to rise. For Gen Z it’s higher still. Around five hours a day in the United States where, for this demographic, social media has also become the primary search engine and shopping tool. Meanwhile, for those who miss what are fast becoming the old days when social media enabled you to share a bit of your life, a joke or a point of view with people you more-or-less knew, there are tools within platforms, says Matt Navarra, that allow you to choose to see mainly friends and family content. "People can flick to a feed that gives them that," he says. "But most people don't." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.   For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 2026年5月22日 分享 保存 在Google上添加为首选 约翰·劳伦森 社交媒体平台过去是关于朋友之间交流的——如今许多平台日益成为短视频娱乐中心。其商业模式是增加人们在应用上花费的时间，并提高广告收入。但消费者是否已经产生了反弹？奥雷利娅给自己冲了杯咖啡，坐在巴黎附近她美丽的花园里，打开Instagram“放松一下”。首先出现的是：“一个我很喜欢的做室内设计的人。他目前在威尼斯。”她热衷室内设计，甚至刚在手臂上纹了两幅19世纪英国设计师威廉·莫里斯的鸟类画作。她继续往下滑。两只小猫在打架。“我喜欢动物，所以我看到很多动物内容。社交媒体就是这样运作的。你点击香蕉，它就给你推香蕉。”还有广告——尽管它们看起来和其他帖子一模一样——推销扫地机器人、减肥方案和床品（带有莫里斯风格设计）。但没有朋友。她在Instagram上有198个好友，但她说“完全变了。我几乎再也看不到朋友的帖子了。”她基本上已经放弃自己发帖了。“反正我觉得也没人看得到了。”尽管Instagram、尤其是Facebook上仍有忠实的社交型业余发帖者，但从与认识的人交流转向浏览不认识的人制作的专业内容，这一趋势在年轻用户中更为明显。16岁的基利安正在接受职业培训，准备成为厨师。他说自己大量使用TikTok和YouTube。“我更喜欢看视频，而不是照片或消息。我看不认识的人做的视频。我完全不发帖。我是个比较害羞的人。我待在自己的泡泡里。我只看，仅此而已。我的反应只留给自己。”同样16岁的露西说：“我花很多时间刷内容创作者做的视频。它们比我认识的人发的帖子更有意思。”她除了偶尔发“快拍”（24小时后消失）之外，也不发帖。无论是TikTok、Snapchat、Facebook还是Instagram，我们都已远离了社交媒体仅仅几年前还是的那种个人互动的“数字城镇广场”。在法国，2026年年度官方《数字晴雨表》显示，49%的社交媒体用户“只是偶尔活跃”。在英国，Ofcom于4月发布的一份报告显示，积极发帖的用户同比从61%下降到49%。在美国，Morning Consult去年6月的一项调查发现，28%的人表示发帖频率低于前一年。如今仅有33%的人每天发帖，而57%的人每天使用社交媒体是为了娱乐。这一差距在Z世代中更大——18%活跃发帖，74%被动浏览。凡妮莎·拉洛是巴黎的一位临床心理学家，专攻网络行为

##段落
他说：“用户越来越意识到，（在社交媒体上）留下的痕迹会永远存在，有些人不再想维持可能很肤浅的社交媒体关系。有些人不希望暴露在批评之下，因为发帖可能带来风险，或者觉得自己的帖子在所有专业内容旁边会显得逊色。”然而，拉洛补充说，人们并没有停止发帖，而是发布不同的内容，并发布在不同的地方。“例如，在TikTok上，年轻人发布大量内容，但更多是搞笑模仿和对现有素材的混剪。目标是让人发笑，而不是告诉别人自己的生活。”她说，这种情况仍然存在，但已经从Instagram和Facebook等社交媒体平台转移到WhatsApp等即时通讯网站。人们也在转向Instagram和Snapchat上的私密群组。“这些地方私密得多，你不会被广告和网红制作的内容轮番轰炸。”她说。“我们看到的是社交媒体正在一分为二，”社交媒体顾问、《Geekout Newsletter》作者马特·纳瓦拉说。“Instagram和TikTok这样的大平台正变得更偏向娱乐和发现。WhatsApp正成为人们真正进行社交的地方。问题在于，这类空间更难让公司赚钱。”小企业主正被推动成为主持人、编辑、趋势观察者和内容创作者，而且还是在真正经营业务之外——马特·纳瓦拉。正是TikTok率先开创了一种算法，从你开始滑动的那一刻就判断你喜欢什么，然后用经过计算、能让你尽可能长时间留在该应用上的内容填满你的信息流。马特·纳瓦拉说，如今，“Meta已经构建了它所谓的AI系统，用于Facebook和Instagram上的非关联内容推荐，这基本上意味着，它们越来越多地向你展示你不关注的人的内容，因为机器认为你会喜欢。它不会偏向判断：这是专业创作者吗？这是品牌吗？这是朋友吗？如果它们能看到你经常与某个朋友互动，你可能会看到更多他们的内容。只是你与谁是朋友、你关注谁，在某种程度上已经变得无关紧要。”这一切都意味着，长期以来利用社交媒体进行免费推广的小企业必须提升水平。“对一些小企业来说，确实存在机会，”马特·纳瓦拉说。“一家面包店、花店、沙龙或本地咖啡馆，如果它们有好的故事、强烈的视觉效果，或者人们想看的幕后内容，仍然可以突围。但这也意味着工作已经改变。小企业主正被推动成为主持人、编辑、趋势观察者和内容创作者，而且还是在

##段落
“实际上，运营这门生意的核心。”社交平台仍然主要依靠广告收入变现。这依然是核心商业模式。而且广告收入还在持续增长——Matt Navarra

##段落
社交媒体正在演变成一种类似电视的被动媒介，只不过是一台会随着你换台而自适应调整的电视。或者说，它对你了解得太深，以至于它拿走了遥控器这件事似乎都没那么重要了。你向平台提供关于自己的信息，平台将其用于商业获利，作为回报，它免费为你提供量身定制、投你所好的内容。从真正的社交媒体向娱乐平台的转变，似乎确实正在产生回报。“社交平台仍然主要依靠广告收入变现。这依然是核心商业模式。而且广告收入还在持续增长，”Matt Navarra说道。全球社交媒体广告收入预计将在2026年达到3170亿美元（2360亿英镑），高于去年的2770亿美元（2060亿英镑）。Meta是最大的赢家。其广告销售额在2025年已经同比增长22%。今年广告销售额预计将达到2430亿美元（1810亿英镑），足以首次超越谷歌。AI驱动的数字广告定向投放正变得越来越高效和精准。“社交平台允许企业将广告嵌入你正在浏览的内容之中。每刷三四条就有一条是广告。而且它们是世界上最好的广告定向引擎。它们对你的兴趣了如指掌，因为知道你看了什么、点赞了什么、互动了什么、关注了什么、在应用的某些板块停留了多长时间，诸如此类，”Navarra说。“所以广告主会进去说：‘我想把广告投给英国30到60岁、对DIY感兴趣的人旁边’，社交平台掌握这些信息，就会相应地投放广告。”价格取决于广告主想要的曝光量（点击量）以及定向条件的精细程度。把广告投放到买马的人的社交媒体信息流中，比投放到买冰淇淋的人的信息流中要贵。

readings.title: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
body: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> Maria Petrishina / iStock

While there are various approaches to leading a team, many of us land on common questions in the search for an effective leadership style: How can I be there for my team? Do I need to command respect, or earn it? And the most crucial question of all: How can I make sure that my team trusts me?

Cady Coleman has been confronting these questions throughout her career as a chemist, engineer, Air Force colonel and astronaut. In conversation with TED science curator David Biello, Coleman shared three strategies to establish — and maintain — trust in a leader. Whatever your career is, these tips can help you to prepare your team to face any challenge you come across — in outer space or here on Earth.
People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team” … But maybe there should be.
1. Be brave enough to get to know your team members as individuals

People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team”… But maybe there should be, says Coleman. Every member of your team is a whole person, and since so many of the problems we face at work are interdisciplinary, understanding who each individual is beyond the 9-to-5 is valuable. Being vulnerable enough to get to know your team this way is an essential skill for any leader.

When you are able to say, “I think your world is different from mine, and I’d like to understand more about it,” you’re not just building trust; you’re opening a communication channel that teaches you more about your teammate’s qualities, says Coleman. This type of conversation requires the willingness and bravery to be vulnerable. Once you know what everyone brings to the table, you can foster the growth of qualities that can lead the team to collective success.

For example, as Coleman prepared for life on the space station, her advisors warned that the long periods of time away from family might be too much to handle. For her, however, this wasn’t a problem — she had been commuting and working away from her family for more than a decade. After sharing her experience, her colleagues realized she’d not only be adaptable to life on the space station, but also she could help others cope with the change, too.
2. Create a culture that’s open to everyone’s ideas
While leaders have to guide their teams, it’s equally important to let everyone know that they can advocate for themselves and bring their own ideas to the table.

Coleman benefitted from such leadership at NASA when she was training to go to the space station. In the face of budget cuts, NASA announced that they’d be eliminating their smaller space suits, meaning that if someone wasn’t qualified to use a larger space suit, they couldn’t go to the space station. This presented a choice for Coleman: wait for NASA to acquire suits that fit her or figure out how she could train in the larger suits. By working with NASA’s decision makers, Coleman was able to shift her training to use the bigger suits. Had she not felt the freedom to speak up, she says, she would have been waiting 10 years to go to the space station in a small suit.
When you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily.

Sometimes establishing trust in the workplace can be more difficult than you expect, but when you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily. Workplace dynamics are always changing — maybe a teammate’s work/life priorities have shifted, or a big mistake requires you all to work together under new pressures. These challenges make fostering trust tricky, but they are also moments of opportunity.

If a new challenge has arisen or trust has been breached, Coleman reminds us to “always figure out the why and the what.” Make sure to ask: why has this happened, why do they feel this way, and what can be done about it? Be open to different points of view, and don’t give up if you don’t get through at first. Connection is often in the smaller things you do; talk about food or music, write a note to compliment an idea and ask to hear more. This level of connection and vulnerability may not seem intuitive at first, but as you make trust a core part of your mission, it becomes easy.

Trust, Coleman reminds us, is both given and earned. As a woman, she knew gaining the trust of some male colleagues might be extra challenging. Her approach was simple: she performed well and, with patience and persistence, learned her colleagues’ language and taught them hers. The challenges in gaining trust will always be there, but if you model vulnerability, openness and understanding for your team, you’ll find the rewards will always be there, too.

This post was adapted from a recent LinkedIn Live conversation with Cady Coleman, former NASA Astronaut and author of the forthcoming book, Sharing Space: An Astronaut’s Guide to Mission, Wonder, and Making Change , due out July 2024.

##段落
领导力究竟是什么样子？
虽然带领团队的方式多种多样，但许多人在寻找高效领导风格的过程中，都会遇到一些共同的问题：我怎样才能为团队提供支持？我需要让人敬畏，还是赢得尊重？而最关键的问题是：我怎样才能确保团队信任我？
##段落
凯迪·科尔曼在她的职业生涯中——作为化学家、工程师、空军上校和宇航员——一直在面对这些问题。在与TED科学策展人大卫·别洛的对话中，科尔曼分享了三个建立并维持领导者信任的策略。无论你从事什么职业，这些建议都能帮助你让团队做好准备，去面对你们遇到的任何挑战——无论是在外太空还是在地球上。
##段落
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我”……但也许应该有。
##段落
1. 勇于把团队成员当作独立的个体去了解
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我'”……但科尔曼认为，也许应该有。你团队中的每个成员都是一个完整的人，而由于我们在工作中面临的许多问题都是跨学科的，了解每个人在朝九晚五之外是谁，是非常有价值的。愿意以这种方式去了解你的团队，是任何领导者必备的一项关键能力。
##段落
科尔曼说，当你能够说出“我觉得你的世界和我的不一样，我想更多地了解它”时，你不仅仅是在建立信任；你还在打开一条沟通渠道，让你更深入地了解队友的特质。这类对话需要你愿意并且敢于展现脆弱。一旦你了解了每个人能带来什么，你就能促进那些能带领团队走向共同成功的品质不断成长。
##段落
例如，当科尔曼为空间站生活做准备时，她的顾问们警告说，长时间远离家人可能让人难以承受。但对她来说，这并不是问题——她已经通勤并在远离家人的情况下工作了十多年。在分享了自己的经历之后，同事们意识到，她不仅能适应空间站的生活，还能帮助其他人应对这种变化。
##段落
2. 创造一种对所有人的想法都保持开放的文化
虽然领导者必须引导团队，但同样重要的是让每个人都知道，他们可以为自己发声，并提出自己的想法。
##段落
科尔曼在美国宇航局接受太空训练时，就受益于这样的领导方式。

## 在预算削减的背景下，NASA宣布将取消较小尺寸的宇航服，这意味着如果某人没有资格使用较大尺寸的宇航服，就无法前往空间站。这给科尔曼带来了一个选择：等待NASA采购适合她的宇航服，或者想办法穿着较大尺寸的宇航服进行训练。通过与NASA决策者合作，科尔曼得以将训练调整为使用较大尺寸的宇航服。她说，如果她没有敢于发声的自由，她可能要等上10年才能穿着小号宇航服前往空间站。

## 当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其余的事情就会水到渠成。

## 3. 把信任作为你的使命

## 有时候，在职场中建立信任可能比你预想的更困难，但当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其余的事情就会水到渠成。职场动态始终在变化——也许某位队友的工作与生活优先级发生了改变，或者一个重大失误要求你们所有人顶着新的压力协同合作。这些挑战让培养信任变得棘手，但它们同样是机遇的时刻。

## 如果出现了新的挑战，或者信任已被破坏，科尔曼提醒我们“始终要弄清楚原因和内容”。确保问自己：为什么会发生这件事？他们为什么会有这种感受？对此能做些什么？对不同观点保持开放心态，如果一开始没有沟通成功，不要放弃。连接往往体现在你做的那些小事上：聊聊美食或音乐，写一张便条称赞某个想法并请对方多说一些。这种程度的连接和脆弱感一开始可能看起来不够直观，但当你把信任作为使命的核心部分时，它就会变得自然而然。

## 科尔曼提醒我们，信任既是给予的，也是赢得的。作为一名女性，她知道赢得某些男同事的信任可能格外具有挑战性。她的方法很简单：她表现出色，并以耐心和坚持学习同事的语言，同时教他们理解自己的语言。赢得信任的挑战永远存在，但如果你为团队示范脆弱、开放和理解，你会发现回报也永远存在。

## 本文改编自最近与凯迪·科尔曼的LinkedIn Live对话。科尔曼是前NASA宇航员，也是即将于2024年7月出版的新书《共享太空：宇航员关于使命、奇迹与推动变革的指南》的作者。

readings.title: Temperature may trump light for shaping sleep
body: 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Amanda Ruggeri Some scientists think that temperature could be just as important as light at training the body's circadian clocks. Even today, anthropologist Gandhi Yetish remembers the bedtime ritual he had as a child during cold New Jersey winters. He would open his window, letting the frigid air rush in and cool his face. He'd quickly feel drowsier, though he'd wonder what his mother would say about the heating bill. There's emerging evidence that Yetish was onto something. From how deeply we sleep to how refreshed we feel afterwards, temperature can have a profound impact on our nightly rest. Some scientists are even going one step further, arguing that temperature may be as important as light for shaping when we sleep. Here's what we do and don't know. For years, Yetish thought his preference for cool sleeping quarters was a personal quirk. Then, while researching the sleep of people in non-industrial societies, he spent time with the Tsimane, an indigenous group in Bolivia's Amazon. Yetish was keenly aware of the long-held scientific consensus that the most important environmental cue for sleep was light exposure. But he found that the Tsimane typically went to sleep hours after sunset and rose before sunrise, despite lacking electricity for artificial lighting and spending most of their days outdoors. Next, Yetish and a team of colleagues from universities across the US investigated the sleep of two other indigenous groups. These included the Hadza of northern Tanzania and the San in Southern Africa. The researchers found that their sleep timings also didn't correspond with light and dark cycles. Instead, it seemed to be tracking the rise and fall of the ambient temperature. "We assume that the reason the sunset and sunrise are important is because of the light," says Yetish. "Well, temperature also comes from the Sun." Decades of evidence shows that our core body temperature begins to drop as we wind down for sleep. For most of us, it continues to decline for much of the night, usually falling by around 1C from its daytime high to nighttime low. How to Sleep Better Want to wake up rested and feel more alert? Sign up to How to Sleep Better , our free six-part email course which features expert tips on how to improve your sleep. This helps explain why people often experience shortened, more disturbed sleep when their room isn't cool enough, says Sebastian Herberger, a sleep physician and scientist at the Interdisciplinary Center of Sleep Medicine in Berlin. "Everyone who's ever slept in a hotel room that's too hot would potentially know these kinds of effects," he says. For a 2007 study , researchers changed the temperature of the room participants slept in to investigate its effects. The group experienced two different sleep set-ups. In one experiment, they were provided with a room where the temperature lowered from 27C (81F) to 24C (75F) from 18:00 to 22:00, slowly rose to 27C between 03:00 and 07:00, and then remained at 27C during the day. This was to mimic the natural rise and fall of the ambient temperature through the night. In the other experiment, they slept in a room at a constant 27C. When they slept in fluctuating temperatures, the participants had higher levels of a marker of melatonin overnight, compared to those who slept at a steady 27C. This hormone is produced by the body naturally, increasing in the lead-up to sleep time and usually reaching its peak in the middle of the night. It tells your body to wind down and prepare for sleep. The same group also felt more refreshed when they awoke. The researchers speculated that we evolved to have deeper sleep under the influence of the natural temperature fluctuations at dusk and dawn.  However, the ideal temperature drop required to drift off to sleep is not yet clear – and how much temperature might impact our body clocks and sleep timings is still being debated.    One question raised by the potential link between temperature and sleep is whether, and how much, it can help to set our internal body clocks. These clocks coordinate our  "circadian rhythms", cycles of mental, physical and behavioural changes that occur in any 24-hour period. This includes everything from when we sleep to when we eat. Circadian rhythms are traditionally thought to be dictated mainly by our exposure to light.    The circadian rhythm is the primary driver behind the fall in our body temperature in the lead-up to sleep, says Russell Foster, professor of circadian neuroscience at the University of Oxford and author of the book Life Time. But Foster explains that temperature may not just be influenced by our body clocks – it may be an extra input that helps shape them, too. "What it's actually doing in terms of as a signal to the sleep systems, we don't know," he says. Animal experiments have provided some evidence for the idea that temperature may itself be helping to set our body clocks. Studies have found that you can train the circadian rhythms of a variety of species, from fruit flies to camels , through fluctuating temperature cycles alone. Scientists have also been able to train the internal clocks of human cells by simulating fluctuating body temperatures. We just don't live in the environment that we've evolved for – Jerome Siegel Animal and cell studies don't necessarily apply to real-life humans, and discerning whether temperature is really a key clock-setter for our species is remarkably difficult. For example, if someone has more trouble sleeping in warmer temperatures, that might have nothing to do with their circadian rhythm. Instead, it may be down to what their body physiologically needs to relax. But the findings of some small studies hint that there could be more to it. In one 1974 study , participants adjusted their room temperature so that it was about 6C (11F) cooler while they were sleeping compared to when they were awake. That change lengthened their sleep-wake cycles by around 23 minutes – meaning that, when it comes to controlling human circadian rhythms, "the effect of temperature is very similar to that of light", the study noted. Meanwhile, a 2007 study found that lowering then increasing the ambient temperature affected the participants' internal body temperature too. The timing of when your body temperature hits its lowest part is an indicator of where you are in your circadian rhythm. The participants exposed to fluctuating temperatures reached that low point about an hour earlier in the night, on average, than when the room temperature stayed constant. This suggests that the temperature of your bedroom can help to set your circadian clocks. But much more research is needed. Temperature may help to modulate our circadian rhythms, says Christian Cajochen, a chronobiologist at the University of Basel. But very few experiments have explored the question. As a result, for now, "in my view, temperature is not the 'new light'" in terms of setting our body clocks, he says. When it comes to temperature's role on sleep, what makes matters more complicated is that sleep is a multi-dimensional physiological process. Two core systems determine when we get sleepy, and how much. The first, the sleep homeostat , means that the longer we are awake, the sleepier we get. The second, the circadian rhythm, is made up of a series of body clocks that time when we feel drowsy and when we are alert. But a third system has an impact, too. This is the " arousal-promoting system", which, in the right circumstances, can override the other systems to keep you awake. This is the reason why a fire alarm is likely to get you out of bed, even if it is 03:00. While all of these systems are linked together, Yetish acknowledges that the sleep patterns he studied in the Tsimane, San and Hadza could have been down to one of these other processes. More like this: •  The blue light from your phone isn't ruining your sleep •  What hunter gatherers can teach us about sleep •  Here's how to catch up on sleep, the right way Jerome Siegel, neuroscientist and director of the Center for Sleep Research at the University of California, Los Angeles, led the research on these indigenous groups. "I think temperature is more important than light," he says. In his view, this has wide implications for modern health. For instance he argues that our tendency to live in homes where the temperature remains the same day and night is likely to contribute to the sleep issues people have in the modern world. This includes the far higher rates of insomnia reported in industrial societies compared to non-industrial ones. When the researchers investigated the prevalence of insomnia among the Tsimane and San, they found that neither group had a word for the condition.    "We just don't live in the environment that we've evolved for," says Siegel. More research is needed to figure out the best way to use temperature to hack your sleep. But for now, opening a window at night like Yetish used to might be worth a try.  *Amanda Ruggeri is a science, psychology and history journalist. She writes the six-part How to Sleep Better newsletter course , and her forthcoming book, The Sleep Myth , will be published in summer 2027. -- For more sleep insight and tips, you might like How to Sleep Better. Our free six-part email course features expert guidance for improving your sleep – and some of the tips may surprise you. Sign up here . 2天前 分享 收藏 在Google上添加为首选 阿曼达·鲁杰里 一些科学家认为，在训练人体生物钟方面，温度可能与光线同等重要。即使在今天，人类学家甘地·耶蒂什仍记得他童年时在新泽西寒冷冬天里的睡前仪式。他会打开窗户，让寒冷的空气涌入，冷却他的脸。他很快就会感到昏昏欲睡，尽管他会想母亲对取暖费会怎么说。有新出现的证据表明，耶蒂什的做法是有道理的。从我们睡得多沉到醒来后感觉多精神，温度对我们的夜间休息有着深远的影响。一些科学家甚至更进一步，认为温度在决定我们何时睡觉方面可能与光线同等重要。以下是我们已知和未知的内容。多年来，耶蒂什一直认为自己偏爱凉爽的睡眠环境是个人怪癖。后来，在研究非工业社会人群的睡眠时，他与玻利维亚亚马逊地区的原住民群体齐曼人共度了一段时间。耶蒂什深知长期以来的科学共识，即对睡眠最重要的环境线索是光照。但他发现，齐曼人通常在日落后数小时才入睡，日出前就起床，尽管他们没有电力供应人工照明，且大部分时间都在户外活动。接下来，耶蒂什和来自美国多所大学的同事团队研究了另外两个原住民族群的睡眠。这些包括坦桑尼亚北部的哈扎人和南部非洲的桑人。研究人员发现，他们的睡眠时间也不与昼夜循环相对应。相反，它似乎是在追踪环境温度的升降。“我们假设日落和日出之所以重要是因为光线，”耶蒂什说。“嗯，温度也来自太阳。”数十年的证据表明，我们的核心体温在准备入睡时开始下降。对我们大多数人来说，它会在夜间大部分时间持续下降，通常从白天的高点降至夜间的低点，降幅约为1摄氏度。如何睡得更好 想要醒来时精神饱满、感觉更警觉吗？注册我们的免费六部分邮件课程《如何睡得更好》，其中包含改善睡眠的专家建议。这有助于解释为什么当房间不够凉爽时，人们经常会经历缩短的、更受干扰的睡眠，柏林跨学科睡眠医学中心的睡眠医生兼科学家塞巴斯蒂安·赫伯格说。“任何曾在太热的酒店房间里睡过觉的人可能都体验过这类影响，”他说。在2007年的一项研究中，研究人员改变了参与者睡觉房间的温度以调查其影响。该组受

##段落
他们体验了两种不同的睡眠环境。在一项实验中，他们被安排在一个房间内，温度从18：00到22：00由27°C降至24°C，在03：00至07：00之间缓慢回升至27°C，白天则保持在27°C。这是为了模拟夜间环境温度的自然升降。在另一项实验中，他们睡在一个恒定27°C的房间里。当参与者在波动的温度中睡眠时，其夜间褪黑素标志物水平高于那些在恒定27°C下睡眠的人。这种激素由人体自然产生，在入睡前逐渐增加，通常在半夜达到峰值。它会告诉你的身体放松下来，准备入睡。同一组人在醒来时也感觉更加精神焕发。研究人员推测，我们在黄昏和黎明自然温度波动的影响下进化出了更深的睡眠。然而，入睡所需的理想温度下降幅度尚不清楚——温度在多大程度上可能影响我们的生物钟和睡眠时间仍存争议。

##段落
温度与睡眠之间的潜在联系引发的一个问题是，它是否以及能在多大程度上帮助设定我们的内部生物钟。这些生物钟协调着我们的“昼夜节律”，即在任何24小时周期内发生的心理、生理和行为变化的循环。这涵盖了我们从何时睡觉到何时进食的一切。传统上认为，昼夜节律主要由我们接触光线的情况所决定。

##段落
牛津大学昼夜节律神经科学教授、《生命时光》一书作者拉塞尔·福斯特表示，昼夜节律是入睡前体温下降的主要驱动因素。但福斯特解释说，温度可能不仅受我们生物钟的影响——它也可能是一种帮助塑造生物钟的额外输入。“就它作为睡眠系统信号的实际作用而言，我们并不清楚，”他说。动物实验为温度本身可能有助于设定生物钟这一观点提供了一些证据。研究发现，仅通过波动温度循环，就可以训练从果蝇到骆驼等多种物种的昼夜节律。科学家们还能够通过模拟波动的体温来训练人类细胞的内部时钟。杰罗姆·西格尔说，我们只是不再生活在我们进化所适应的环境中了。动物和细胞研究不一定适用于现实中的人类，而要辨别温度是否真的是我们物种的关键生物钟设定因素，则异常困难。例如，如果有人在较高温度下更难入睡，那可能与此无关。

与他们的昼夜节律无关。相反，这可能取决于他们身体生理上放松所需的条件。但一些小型研究的结果暗示，事情可能远不止如此。在1974年的一项研究中，参与者在睡眠时将室温调至比清醒时低约6摄氏度（11华氏度）。这一变化使他们的睡眠-觉醒周期延长了约23分钟——研究指出，这意味着在调控人类昼夜节律方面，"温度的作用与光照非常相似"。与此同时，2007年的一项研究发现，先降低再升高环境温度也会影响参与者的体内温度。体温降至最低点的时机是判断你处于昼夜节律哪个阶段的指标。暴露于波动温度中的参与者在夜间平均比室温恒定时提前约一小时达到体温最低点。这表明卧室温度可能有助于设定你的昼夜节律钟。但还需要更多的研究。巴塞尔大学时间生物学家克里斯蒂安·卡约兴表示，温度可能有助于调节我们的昼夜节律。但很少有实验探讨过这个问题。因此，就设定人体生物钟而言，"在我看来，温度并不是'新的光照'"，他说。当涉及温度对睡眠的作用时，让事情更加复杂的是，睡眠是一个多维度的生理过程。两个核心系统决定了我们何时感到困倦以及困倦的程度。第一个是睡眠稳态系统，意味着我们醒着的时间越长，就越困。第二个是昼夜节律，由一系列体内生物钟组成，负责计时我们何时感到昏昏欲睡、何时处于警觉状态。但第三个系统也有影响。这就是"促觉醒系统"，在适当的情况下，它可以凌驾于其他系统之上，让你保持清醒。这就是为什么火警很可能让你从床上爬起来，即使是在凌晨三点。虽然所有这些系统相互关联，但耶蒂什承认，他在齐马内人、桑人和哈扎人中研究的睡眠模式可能归因于其中其他某个过程。更多相关内容：• 手机发出的蓝光并不会破坏你的睡眠 • 狩猎采集者能教给我们关于睡眠的哪些事 • 以下是如何以正确方式补觉。加州大学洛杉矶分校神经科学家兼睡眠研究中心主任杰罗姆·西格尔领导了对这些原住民群体的研究。"我认为温度比光照更重要，"他说。在他看来，这对现代健康具有广泛意义。例如，他认为我们倾向于居住在恒温环境中的习惯

readings.title: The Trump administration plans a public killing
body: Politics / Donald Trump / The Logoff The Trump administration plans a public killing ﻿Pete Hegseth’s “barbaric” plan for a livestreamed execution, briefly explained. by Cameron Peters Oct 9, 2026, 10:40 PM UTC Gift Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks from a stage in Sparrows Point, Maryland, on October 6, 2026. Win McNamee/Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here . Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is planning a public killing. What’s happening? On Thursday, the Pentagon announced that it would execute Nidal Hasan, a former Army major sentenced to death for a 2009 mass shooting on a military base, publicly and on livestream. The execution, if it happens, would be unprecedented: The last widely reported public execution in the US was 90 years ago , in Kentucky, but to stream a death live would be something else entirely. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has promoted the announcement with something approaching glee, telling a reporter that “we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.” What’s the context? According to the Pentagon, Hasan will be executed via firing squad on December 3 — the first such execution by the military in more than 80 years. Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death in 2013 by a military jury following a court-martial for the 2009 shooting, when he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 at Fort Hood in Texas. The execution is set to be carried out at the same Army post. Will the Pentagon go through with this? It’s unclear, for multiple reasons. The Pentagon’s announcement that Hasan’s death will be livestreamed has generated a great deal of bipartisan pushback, as well as condemnation by religious groups , though that is unlikely to stop the execution itself. The head of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops decried the decision to livestream the execution as “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death,” and retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) called it the decision “beyond disgusting.” “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do,” Tillis wrote in a post on X. On Friday, Vice President JD Vance also said that he was unsure if the livestream would take place . Hasan’s legal team could also delay the execution substantially — potentially for multiple years — by challenging his detention in federal court, though he has exhausted the military appeals process. ##政治 / 唐纳德·特朗普 / 下线简报 特朗普政府计划进行一场公开处决 皮特·赫格塞思“野蛮”的直播处决计划，简要说明。 作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯 2026年10月9日，晚上10:40 UTC 赠阅 国防部长皮特·赫格塞思于2026年10月6日在马里兰州斯帕罗斯角的一个舞台上发表讲话。温·麦克纳米/盖蒂图片社 卡梅伦·彼得斯是Vox的特约编辑。本文发表于《下线简报》，这是一份每日通讯，帮助你了解特朗普政府的动态，而不让政治新闻占据你的生活。点此订阅。

##欢迎来到《下线简报》：特朗普政府正在计划一场公开处决。 发生了什么？ 周四，五角大楼宣布将对尼达尔·哈桑执行死刑，公开且以直播方式进行。哈桑是一名前陆军少校，因2009年在军事基地制造大规模枪击事件被判处死刑。这次处决如果付诸实施，将是史无前例的：美国上一次被广泛报道的公开处决是在90年前的肯塔基州，但直播一场死亡则完全是另一回事。国防部长皮特·赫格塞思以一种近乎欢欣鼓舞的态度宣传了这一消息，他对一名记者说：“我们会确保人们能够观看。”

##背景是什么？ 据五角大楼称，哈桑将于12月3日被行刑队处决——这是80多年来军方首次采用这种处决方式。哈桑曾是陆军精神科医生，因2009年在得克萨斯州胡德堡枪杀13人、致30多人受伤，于2013年被军事法庭陪审团判处死刑。处决将在同一陆军基地执行。

##五角大楼会真的执行吗？ 目前尚不清楚，原因有多方面。五角大楼宣布哈桑的死刑将被直播后，引发了大量两党反对声音，以及宗教团体的谴责，尽管这不太可能阻止处决本身。美国天主教主教会议主席谴责直播处决的决定是“对死亡文化的野蛮推广”，即将退休的参议员汤姆·蒂利斯（北卡罗来纳州共和党人）称这一决定“令人作呕到极点”。“公开处决是伊朗和阿富汗这类压迫性独裁政权才会做的事，”蒂利斯在X平台上发帖写道。周五，副总统JD·万斯也表示，他不确定直播是否会进行。哈桑的法律团队也可能通过在联邦法院质疑其拘留来大幅推迟处决——可能推迟数年——尽管他已经用尽了军事上诉程序。

readings.title: The real history behind the philosophers' stone
body: 16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Sophie Hardach The myth of Nicolas and Pernelle Flamel, medieval Parisians said to have made gold with a 'philosopher's stone', sparked a centuries-long obsession. Now a new examination of Flamel's centuries-old will has shed a light on how the legend emerged. For 600 years, writers, artists and scientists have been fascinated by the legend of Nicolas and Pernelle Flamel: a medieval Parisian couple who were said to have created the mythical philosophers' stone, a mysterious substance that supposedly turned ordinary metals into gold. Flamel, a real person who was born in the 1330s and died in 1418, in fact never had anything to do with the practice of alchemy, the ancient, mystical tradition which aimed to create gold, cure all diseases and bring immortality. Still, Flamel's mythical reputation as an alchemist inspired generations of scientists and writers including Isaac Newton , Victor Hugo , and JK Rowling, who mentions Nicolas and Pernelle Flamel in Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone. This autumn, the will of Nicolas Flamel is on public display for the first time at a new exhibition at the Musée de Cluny  in Paris. Stored in a Parisian hospital archive for centuries, the document sheds a new light on how he ended up being revered as an alchemist, says Maëlys Bitouzet, one of the curators of the exhibition. "They were documents that had never been studied," until the museum evaluated them in 2024, says Bitouzet. The quest to uncover why Flamel became known as an alchemist also sheds light on the enduring appeal of this ancient tradition, and its sometimes-overlooked place in the history of science. The first alchemical writings appeared around 2,000 years ago in ancient Egypt . Through copies and translations, they spread to Europe in the 12th Century with the Islamic Conquest. The word "alchemy" is thought to be an Arabic-Greek hybrid, with an unclear meaning – it could refer to melting or to Egypt. Alchemy used routes which we now know are not scientifically viable, though some of the elusive aims have since been achieved in very fleeting, experimental set-ups . Throughout its history, alchemists wrote about their efforts to create an enigmatic, powerful stone. "The earliest reference to ' the stone of the philosophers' is in the 7th Century, in a Byzantine text," in the eastern Mediterranean, says Matteo Martelli, a professor in history of science at the University of Bologna in Italy and expert on ancient alchemical texts. "'The philosophers' were what alchemists called themselves." The concept of the stone appears even earlier, in a text dating from the 1st Century BC, where the author "refers to a stone that is not a stone ", says Martelli. "There is this cryptic way of talking about this stone, which was later called the philosophers' stone," he adds, noting it wasn't literally a stone, but came in different forms such as a powder or liquid. The stone was meant to turn other metals into gold or silver, not necessarily for personal gain, but as a way of perfecting nature, says Martelli. In medieval Europe, an additional belief grew that the stone would bring health benefits and even immortality. This is where Flamel enters the history of alchemy. Traces of Flamel's real life are dotted around Paris, including his tombstone, which is a visitor magnet at the Musée de Cluny, France's National Museum of the Middle Ages. "In the [Harry Potter] book, Flamel is an alchemist, a sorcerer, so it's surprising to people that there's a real tombstone, and that Flamel was a real person," says Bitouzet. In the late 15th Century, some 50-75 years after his death, an alchemical text known as Le Livre Flamel (The Flamel Book) was published in France – the first alchemical manuscript published under the name "Flamel". While it was actually by an anonymous author, not the real Nicolas Flamel, it became a huge success. "[Le Livre Flamel] was very popular, it was re-copied, and then people really began to associate it with [the real] Nicolas Flamel," says Bitouzet. Over the centuries, other writings appeared under his name , sometimes including detailed real facts about Nicolas and Pernelle Flamel's life in Paris, such as where they had lived. The first Livre Flamel, from the late 15th Century, describes a step-by-step alchemical procedure that results in a liquid, Bitouzet says. According to the book, immersing lead into this liquid transforms it into gold. "It talks about the theory of alchemy, how one can help metals reach a purer state. And then it really gives you the practical recipe [for a philosophers' stone], as if Flamel is giving you little tips to make your philosophers' stone a success," says Bitouzet. Martelli, who has seen the original, 15th-Century Livre Flamel, notes that some of the procedures and ingredients are the same as those in the much older, Eastern manuscripts. In other words, while the attribution to Flamel was fake, the recipe did tap into genuine alchemical history. So why did someone copy ancient alchemical instructions, then publish them under the name of a real, dead person? Flamel's will, and other documents and artefacts, have shed a new light on this mystery. The last will and testament and related documents had been kept in the archive of the Hôpital des Quinze-Vingts in Paris, which specialises in eye disease and dates to 1260. Flamel was one of the hospital's benefactors and included it in his will.  "They were documents that had never been studied," until the museum evaluated them in 2024, says Bitouzet. A man who was rich, who was not aristocratic, but who had a high social standing – people found that strange – Maëlys Bitouzet Other historical records and monuments already painted a picture of Flamel as a wealthy property owner who donated to churches and charities. But the newly studied documents show that his investments and impact were far bigger than had previously been assumed, says Bitouzet. "He really had a real-estate empire," says Bitouzet. "Before [the discovery of the will and related documents], we vaguely knew that he owned a lot of real estate, but we didn't know exactly what he owned and where these houses were."  Flamel was the creditor of hundreds of property owners in and around Paris, and himself owned around 10 houses, according to the documents, Bitouzet says. His will stipulated various charitable donations and shows him making detailed arrangements for joint Masses to be read for him and his wife after his death (Pernelle had died earlier than him). These Masses continued for centuries, until the eve of the French Revolution in 1789. After Flamel's death, a legal battle over his inheritance put his wealth in the spotlight. This combination of fame, wealth and philanthropy could explain why people thought Flamel was an alchemist, Bitouzet says. "A man who was rich, who was not aristocratic, but who had a high social standing – people found that strange," Bitouzet says. Alchemy – seen then as a way of doing God's work – could have explained his wealth, charitable donations and seemingly blessed life, she adds. As early as the 1700s , some questioned whether Flamel was really the author of the texts in his name, but it didn't stop the interest in him. Real-life reminders of Flamel may have helped keep the legend alive. A house built by the Flamels in 1407 and offered as shelter to the poor stands in the Rue Montmorency to this day – it's one of the oldest houses in Paris. Recreating a 'philosophers' stone' Scientists today are trying to replicate ancient alchemical recipes to shed a light on their real chemical processes. In 2024, Martelli and others reproduced one for a philosophers' stone : based on eggs, it resulted in a powder. Lucia Maini, a professor in chemistry at the University of Bologna who collaborated on the project, points out that eggs, which contain sulphur, can react with silver and give it a golden sheen – which could explain why alchemists thought they had found a way to make gold. "They were trying to understand nature by observation," says Maini, who sees alchemy as a precursor to chemistry. Pernelle is also mentioned in the writings published under Flamel's name as a virtuous woman who worked with Nicolas, and who would have also been able to create a philosophers' stone if she had wanted to, says Bitouzet.   Martelli points out that publishing texts under the names of famous people, a phenomenon called pseudo-epigraphy, was common from the earliest days of alchemy. "Pseudo-epigraphy is a feature of the alchemical tradition," he says. "So what happens with Flamel is a mechanism that we can see in many moments in the history of alchemy. It's just to make a text more authoritative, more legitimate."  More like this: • For 1,000 years, a cult worshipped the hero of the Odyssey • Our 2,500-year-old mania for personality types • The ancient reason there are 60 minutes in an hour The broader quest to produce the philosophers' stone did lead to scientific breakthroughs. For example, phosphorus was first isolated in the 17th Century by a German alchemist trying to find the philosophers' stone.  Today, though, the main reason Flamel continues to fascinate people is his immortal life in books and art, says Bitouzet. "The legend of Flamel is so strong that people don't want to give up on it, even when they know he wasn't an alchemist," she says. Nicolas Flamel : Alchemist of Paper runs at the Musée de Cluny (Musée national du Moyen Âge) in Paris from 13 Oct 2026 to 24 Jan 2027. --  If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram .  History Science Chemistry Myth Exhibition Features

##段落
16小时前 分享 收藏 在Google上添加为首选 索菲·哈达赫 中世纪巴黎人所说的用“哲人石”制造黄金的尼古拉·弗拉梅尔与佩尔内勒·弗拉梅尔神话，引发了长达数世纪的痴迷。如今，对弗拉梅尔数百年前遗嘱的新研究，为这一传说的形成提供了新的线索。

##段落
600年来，作家、艺术家和科学家一直着迷于尼古拉·弗拉梅尔与佩尔内勒·弗拉梅尔的传说：这对中世纪巴黎夫妇据说制造出了神话中的哲人石——一种据称能把普通金属变成黄金的神秘物质。弗拉梅尔确有其人，生于14世纪30年代，卒于1418年，但实际上他与炼金术实践毫无关系。炼金术是一种古老而神秘的传统，旨在制造黄金、治愈百病并带来永生。尽管如此，弗拉梅尔作为炼金术士的神话声誉仍激励了一代又一代科学家和作家，包括艾萨克·牛顿、维克多·雨果和J·K·罗琳——罗琳在《哈利·波特与魔法石》中提到了尼古拉·弗拉梅尔与佩尔内勒·弗拉梅尔。

##段落
今年秋天，尼古拉·弗拉梅尔的遗嘱首次在巴黎克吕尼博物馆的一场新展览中公开展出。展览策展人之一迈莉丝·比图泽表示，这份文件在巴黎一家医院的档案中保存了数百年，为理解他如何最终被尊为炼金术士提供了新的线索。比图泽说：“这些文件此前从未被研究过”，直到博物馆于2024年对其进行了评估。探寻弗拉梅尔为何被称为炼金术士，也揭示了这一古老传统的持久吸引力，以及它在科学史中有时被忽视的地位。

##段落
最早一批炼金术著作约在2000年前出现在古埃及。通过抄写和翻译，它们随伊斯兰征服于12世纪传入欧洲。“炼金术”一词被认为是阿拉伯语与希腊语的混合体，含义并不明确——它可能指熔化，也可能指埃及。炼金术使用的路径如今我们知道在科学上并不可行，尽管其中一些难以实现的目标后来已在非常短暂、实验性的条件下被达成。在其整个历史中，炼金术士都曾记述他们为制造一种神秘而强大的石头所做的努力。

##段落
意大利博洛尼亚大学科学史教授、古代炼金术文本专家马泰奥·马尔泰利说：“对‘哲人之石’最早的提及是在7世纪的一份拜占庭文本中”，地点在东地中海地区。“‘哲人’是炼金术士对自己的称呼。”这种石头的概念出现得更早，可追溯到公元前1世纪的一份文本，马尔泰利说，其作者“提到了一种不是石头的石头”。“这是一种隐晦的谈论方式……”

##段落
“是石头，后来被称为哲人石，”他补充道，并指出它并非字面意义上的石头，而是以粉末或液体等不同形态出现。马泰利说，这种石头旨在将其他金属变成金或银，不一定是为了个人利益，而是作为一种完善自然的方式。在中世纪欧洲，又多了另一种信念，认为这种石头会带来健康益处，甚至长生不老。弗拉梅尔正是由此进入炼金术史的。弗拉梅尔真实生活的痕迹散落在巴黎各处，包括他的墓碑；这块墓碑是克吕尼博物馆的吸客亮点，该馆是法国国立中世纪博物馆。“在《哈利·波特》书里，弗拉梅尔是一位炼金术士、巫师，所以人们会惊讶地发现真有一块墓碑，而且弗拉梅尔真有其人，”比图泽说。15世纪晚期，也就是他去世后大约50至75年，一部名为《弗拉梅尔之书》的炼金术文本在法国出版——这是第一部以“弗拉梅尔”之名出版的炼金术手稿。虽然它实际上出自一位匿名作者，而非真实的尼古拉·弗拉梅尔，却大获成功。“《弗拉梅尔之书》非常流行，被反复抄录，随后人们真的开始把它与真实的尼古拉·弗拉梅尔联系起来，”比图泽说。几个世纪以来，其他作品也以他的名义出现，有时还包含关于尼古拉和佩雷内尔·弗拉梅尔在巴黎生活的详细真实事实，比如他们曾住在哪里。比图泽说，15世纪晚期的第一部《弗拉梅尔之书》描述了一套循序渐进的炼金术流程，最终得到一种液体。根据该书，将铅浸入这种液体中，就能把它变成黄金。“它谈到炼金术理论，谈人如何帮助金属达到更纯净的状态。然后它真的给出了制作哲人石的实用配方，仿佛弗拉梅尔在给你一些小窍门，让你的哲人石制作成功，”比图泽说。马泰利看过15世纪《弗拉梅尔之书》的原件，并指出其中一些程序和成分与更古老的东方手稿相同。换句话说，虽然托名弗拉梅尔是假的，但那份配方确实接入了真实的炼金术历史。那么，为什么有人会抄录古代炼金术指示，然后以一位真实死者的名义出版呢？弗拉梅尔的遗嘱以及其他文件和文物为这一谜团提供了新的线索。那份最后的遗嘱及相关文件一直保存在巴黎十五二十医院档案馆中；这家医院专治眼病，历史可追溯到1260年。弗拉梅尔是该医院的捐助人之一，并在遗嘱中提到了它。比图泽说，“这些文件此前从未被研究过”，直到博物馆在2024年对它们进行评估。一个

##段落
他富有，却并非贵族，却拥有很高的社会地位——人们觉得这很奇怪——玛埃莉丝·比图泽。其他历史记录和纪念碑早已勾勒出弗拉梅尔的形象：一位富有的地产主，向教堂和慈善机构捐款。但比图泽说，新研究的文件显示，他的投资和影响远比此前设想的要大。“他确实拥有一个房地产帝国，”比图泽说。“在[发现遗嘱及相关文件]之前，我们模糊地知道他拥有大量房产，但不知道他具体拥有什么，以及这些房子在哪里。”

##段落
比图泽说，根据这些文件，弗拉梅尔是巴黎及其周边数百名业主的债权人，他自己拥有约10处房屋。他的遗嘱规定了各种慈善捐赠，并显示他为死后自己和妻子（佩尔内勒先于他去世）的联合弥撒做了详细安排。这些弥撒持续了数个世纪，直到1789年法国大革命前夕。弗拉梅尔死后，一场围绕其遗产的法律争斗将他的财富推到了聚光灯下。

##段落
比图泽说，这种名声、财富和慈善的结合，可以解释为什么人们认为弗拉梅尔是炼金术士。“一个富有、并非贵族、却拥有很高社会地位的人——人们觉得这很奇怪，”比图泽说。她补充说，炼金术——当时被视为践行上帝旨意的一种方式——本可以解释他的财富、慈善捐赠和看似蒙福的人生。

##段落
早在18世纪，就有人质疑弗拉梅尔是否真的是那些以他名义流传的文本的作者，但这并未阻止人们对他的兴趣。弗拉梅尔在现实生活中的遗迹，可能有助于让传说延续。弗拉梅尔夫妇于1407年建造、用作穷人庇护所的一所房子，至今仍矗立在蒙莫朗西街——它是巴黎最古老的房屋之一。

##段落
重现“贤者之石”。如今，科学家们正试图复现古代炼金术配方，以揭示其真实的化学过程。2024年，马尔泰利等人复现了一种贤者之石的配方：以鸡蛋为基础，最终得到一种粉末。参与该项目的博洛尼亚大学化学教授露西娅·迈尼指出，鸡蛋含有硫，可以与银发生反应，使其呈现金色光泽——这或许可以解释为什么炼金术士认为自己找到了制造黄金的方法。“他们试图通过观察来理解自然，”迈尼说。她将炼金术视为化学的前身。

##段落
比图泽说，在以弗拉梅尔名义出版的著作中，佩尔内勒也被提到，称她是一位与尼古拉共同工作的贤德女性，如果她愿意，也本可以制造出贤者之石。

##李指出，以名人名义发表文本——这种现象被称为伪经——从炼金术最早的日子起就很常见。“伪经是炼金术传统的一个特征，”他说。“所以弗拉梅尔身上发生的事，是一种我们在炼金术历史上许多时刻都能看到的机制。它只是为了让一部文本更具权威性、更合法。”

##更多类似内容：• 1000年来，一个教派崇拜《奥德赛》的英雄 • 我们对人格类型长达2500年的痴迷 • 一小时有60分钟的上古原因

##对制造贤者之石的更广泛追求确实带来了科学突破。例如，磷最早是在17世纪由一位试图寻找贤者之石的德国炼金术士分离出来的。

##不过，比图泽说，今天弗拉梅尔继续令人们着迷的主要原因，是他在书籍和艺术中的不朽生命。“弗拉梅尔的传说如此强大，以至于人们不愿放弃它，即使他们知道他不是炼金术士，”她说。尼古拉·弗拉梅尔：纸上的炼金术士将于2026年10月13日至2027年1月24日在巴黎克吕尼博物馆（国立中世纪博物馆）展出。--

readings.title: 6 ways to give that aren’t about money
body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

好消息：你不必开一堆支票也能成为一个慷慨的人。事实上，许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨之举，都是时间与精力、才华与爱心的馈赠，并且是针对特定需求量身定制的。这种付出对每个人都是敞开的。

##段落
许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨之举，都是时间与精力、才华与爱心的馈赠，并且是针对特定需求量身定制的。

##段落
不知道从哪里开始？以下是六种时间与关注的馈赠，它们极有可能引发影响数百万人的涟漪效应，出自TED负责人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。

##段落
1. 转移注意力

##段落
禅宗大师一行禅师曾教导说，注意力是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。慷慨正是从这里开始——愿意停止聚焦于自己，转而关注他人及其需求。从这种联结的行为出发，任何事情都可能发生。

##段落
事实是，这并不容易。我们把大量时间耗费在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿去关注他人正在面对的问题。于是我们竖起盾牌。而这意味着，许多真正需要我們关注的人，从未感到被我们看见。因此，注意力的慷慨，就是愿意让自己稍微不舒服、放下那些盾牌、付出一些时间、冒险去关心他人的慷慨。

##段落
无论你是停下来与一个需要帮助的人建立有意义的联结，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的议题，你都已经踏上了自己的慷慨之旅。

##段落
2. 搭建桥梁

##段落
在我们这个互联时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触那些与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端都在公开的网络上上演。庞大的受众会紧盯网络骂战。如果我们能为更多这类冲突带来令人满意的解决，会怎样？

##段落
主动接触批评我们的人很难。这是一种尤其具有挑战性的慷慨心态。你是在牺牲个人的舒适，以换取把人们聚在一起的更大善果。但如果你成功了，就会有一个强大的连锁益处：你正在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。那是给我们所有人的礼物。

##段落
我们能给予的最伟大的单一礼物就是知识——能解决问题、满足需求或开辟前路的知
识。

##段落
3. 分享知识

##段落
在无数情境中，我们能给予的最伟大的单一礼物就是知识——能解决问题、满足需求或开辟前路的知识。

##段落
我们给某人的最重要的一条建议

##段落
在TED舞台上演讲，意味着演讲者不应将演讲视为推销某样东西（比如企业或事业）的机会，而应将其视为一份礼物。这是一个自由地与观众分享宝贵想法的机会。而这些想法有可能在未来数年里持续影响听众的人生。

##段落
如果你拥有能让他人受益的知识，不妨想想如何将其分享出去，以产生涟漪效应。你花几个小时准备和付诸行动的事情，可能点亮某个人的人生——而这或许仅仅是开始。

##段落
4. 促成连接

在我们这个互联的时代，我们所能触及的人脉网络比以往任何时候都更加重要。因此，最具传播力的慷慨行为之一，就是帮助人们与他人建立联系。最简单的方式就是做一次引荐。

##段落
正如心理学家、TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所言，引荐这件事，给出时相当容易，收到时却价值不可估量。如果你去问很多人他们是如何遇到伴侣、获得理想工作，或为创意项目找到完美合作者的，答案往往如出一辙：某个人——朋友、邻居、同事——把他们介绍给了对的人。你实际上做的，是让别人得以接入你的资源网络。而这些引荐可能产生指数级的连锁效应。

##段落
5. 传递好客之道

人类学家唐纳德·布朗在其杰出著作《人类共性》中记录道，好客是被研究过的每一种文化中都观察到的数百种人类行为之一。但既然好客如此普遍（又如此令人愉悦），它真的算是一种慷慨吗？答案是肯定的。且不说其中涉及的任何花费，光是邀请别人来家里做客——无论是朋友还是可能成为朋友的人——就需要付出心力。窝在沙发里继续追你正在看的剧，显然轻松得多。

##段落
那么，好客如何能推动慷慨的传染？好客触及的是我们内心深处对彼此连接的渴望。而每一次被好客以待的经历，都会唤起一种想要回报的愿望。

##段落
人们需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗，这毋庸置疑。但我们同样渴望美、惊奇、欢笑、超越——这些都是魅力的组成部分。

##段落
6. 创造魅力

先锋艺术家莉莉·叶受邀于舞蹈家兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔，在她家乡费城一块荒废的空地上开展一个社区艺术项目。“我很感兴趣，但完全被吓到了，”叶回忆道。“我资源匮乏，也没有在社区环境中进行户外工作的经验。我想逃跑，但我不想在镜子里看到一个懦夫。于是我迈出了这一步。”

##段落
这个社区项目后来成为了“艺术与人文村”，一座满是树木、雕塑和马赛克的艺术公园，由当地居民共同创造。

##与Yeh合作，为成年人和儿童创作。Yeh的作品让她深刻意识到：在公共空间创造美，对社区具有深远的疗愈和变革力量。
##人们确实需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑、超越——这些都是魅力的元素。能够施展魅力的人，能赠予他人一份无价之礼。

readings.title: Is New York's cannabis business flying high?
body: 26 March 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Mike Wendling Five years after it was legalised in the state, cannabis is seemingly everywhere in New York. But, business owners say that many legitimate outlets are struggling – largely because of a thriving grey market, and the complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry. If you've recently visited New York, you've probably noticed something.  Advertisements outside bodegas display pictures of bright green flowers, higher-end dispensaries that resemble coffee bars or electronics shops welcome customers from all over the world, and then of course there's the smell – so seemingly omnipresent that even US Open tennis players have complained .  Weed is everywhere. From the outside it looks like a free-for-all, one that is drawing scepticism even from voices broadly supportive of the aims of the legalisation – including reducing harm and boosting tax revenue. Social media is rife with complaints (typical comments include "New York could not have screwed up legal weed any worse!") and for years the local press has been chronicling the rise of the "weed bodega" – typically a corner store selling products of dubious provenance. Across the country, weed consumption has increased – though studies indicate  that the rate of young people using has gradually declined since the turn of the century.  Things may have come to a head recently when the  New York Times , once a legal weed supporter, published an editorial headlined: "Marijuana Is Everywhere. That's a Problem." The newspaper now argues that "marijuana is causing more harm than predicted" and calls for tighter regulation.  But this new green rush is not as straightforward as it seems. Business owners say that public perceptions have been sullied by illegal operators, and that many above-board businesses are struggling – largely because of the incredibly complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry.  "At first glance, New York's cannabis industry appears to be booming," says Jayson Tantalo, a cannabis businessman and vice president of operations for the New York Cannabis Retail Association. "But that perception was initially driven by an oversaturation of illicit operators.  "These shops often presented themselves as legitimate, creating a misleading sense of scale and economic success," he says.  New York state legalised recreational use of cannabis five years ago this month . But legal wrangling and slow issuing of licenses hampered initial growth, while sales in other states such as California were racing ahead.   The bottleneck was so restrictive that some growers in New York complained that their crops were going to waste because of the lack of retail sales outlets. Meanwhile hundreds of those shady outlets sprang up, particularly in New York City.  Those wild days may be coming to an end. State authorities are starting to crack down on illegal operators, and police have been given power to immediately shut shops without a licence. And more legal businesses are being set up to address pent-up demand.  "It was really out of control," says Vlad Bautista, co-founder of Happy Munkey, a cannabis retailer in the Inwood neighbourhood of Manhattan.  "It made a little dent," he says of recent enforcement efforts. "But there’s still a long way to go." CRB Monitor, a firm that researches the cannabis industry, counts more than 2,000 active cannabis business licenses across the state – including retailers, wholesalers, growers and other types of cannabis companies – with another nearly 5,000 applications in the pipeline.  The effects can be seen far from Manhattan with weed shops popping up all across a state that is roughly the size of England.  Jayson Tantalo owns one of them. He was involved in the weed business long before it was legal. "What started as survival evolved into deep expertise in the industry," he says. He and his wife Britni set up their Flower City Dispensary retail business in Victor, a suburban community in western New York state with a population of about 16,000.  Tantalo says that while the industry is "highly visible and normalised" across the state, only a small percentage of legal operators have captured large shares of the market.  "Growth exists, but it's constrained, uneven, and still stabilising," he says.  New York's growing pains are just one example of the extraordinarily complicated legal status of cannabis that has caused confusion across the country - for businesses, customers and the public.  The patchwork legal regime around the industry is a product of cannabis's long strange trip from respectability to contraband and back again. George Washington, the first US president, famously grew hemp crops at his estate.   But waves of restrictions followed, culminating in a 1970 law that deemed marijuana a Schedule I drug – the most restrictive category.  Despite the US government's war on drugs, there has always been a significant movement calling for looser regulations on cannabis. That movement gradually became more mainstream in the early years of this century.  Support for legalising cannabis first cracked 50% of Americans in 2013, according to polling firm Gallup, and that figure has since risen to more than two-thirds today.  But instead of blanket legalisation, reforms came in piecemeal fashion, on the state and sometimes even the local level, creating a fragmented state-by-state market.  To top it off, weed remains illegal under federal law – thousands of people still get arrested each year for marijuana possession and related crimes.  This legal patchwork results in some bizarre consequences. A road-tripper heading west from New York would pass through Pennsylvania, where recreational use of marijuana is illegal, and then into Ohio, where it was legalised by a 2023 referendum. If they continued along Interstate 80 they would eventually get to Indiana (where weed is illegal), Illinois (legal), and Iowa (illegal) – and so on.  That's confusing in itself. But another legal loophole has opened the door for all sorts of grey-market and online businesses, effectively making cannabis accessible to nearly everyone in the country.  The 2018 Farm Bill legalised hemp with a relatively low level of tetrahydrocannabinol or THC – the chemical that gets cannabis users high.  Hemp contains CBD – a chemical that doesn’t produce the high of THC but has some health benefits. A glut of CBD ensued. And in a lab, CBD can be converted into psychoactive THC.  "Entrepreneurs could say, 'this is just hemp', even if what they were producing was a highly intoxicating form of THC," says Chris Lindsay, vice president of policy and state advocacy for the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp (ATACH), which represents licenced businesses.  Those products are sold online or in those weed bodegas – even in states that have not legalised marijuana.  Robin Goldstein, an economist at the University of California-Davis and co-author of the book Can Legal Weed Win?: The Blunt Realities of Cannabis Economics, estimates that just behind California, the second-biggest weed market is in Texas, despite the Lone Star state's blanket ban on recreational cannabis use.  Business owners like Jason Ambrosino, have become used to dealing with spiralling legal complexities.  Ambrosino is founder and chief executive of Veterans Holdings, a weed business based in Gloversville, New York, about three hours north of New York City. An army vet who was seriously injured in Iraq, he got into the cannabis industry after discovering that medical marijuana was effective in alleviating his pain. These days, he says his legal headaches include rules that make it impossible to branch out into neighbouring states or to obtain traditional sources of financing.  "There’s a million different ways to get institutional funding, but you can’t get any of those for cannabis because of federal law," he says.  Despite the headwinds, Ambrosino has managed to grow his business and now employs around 80 people, and is hopeful that the increased licences for legal shops in New York will mean more sales opportunities down the line.  Vlad Bautista, the Happy Munkey co-founder, roughly estimates that he spends 40% of his time complying with various regulations, and, in particular, he questions some of the rules around advertising and tax law.  "If you own a cannabis business, you have much stricter advertising regulations than companies selling alcohol, cigarettes or gambling," he says. "You're stuck in the stone age, handing out flyers on the street." A buzz ran through the industry in December of last year, when President Trump signed an executive order which directed officials to accelerate efforts to reclassify marijuana to a less stringent category.  That might eventually give cannabis businesses some added profits – due to another federal law, weed companies aren't able to deduct all of their normal business expenses from their taxes. But businesspeople and experts aren't holding their breath for a practical impact any time soon.  "It's smoke and mirrors," says Naomi Granger, founder and chief executive of the National Association of Cannabis Accounting and Tax Professionals, who says some headlines heralding a new dawn for the cannabis industry have been somewhat misleading.  Some industry insiders say uncertainty is part and parcel of a nascent industry.  Steve Kemmerling, founder and chief executive of CRB Monitor, notes that states that were earlier to legal weed – California and Colorado in the western US were among the first – experienced hiccups on the way to relative stability.  "In any new market you're going to have wild volatility and price swings, mergers and acquisitions, along with competitive businesses and people cutting corners," he says.  And in a buzzy industry perhaps it's not surprising to encounter businesspeople who seem hard wired for sunny-day thinking.  "I'm an optimist," says Vlad Bautista. "We live in a divided and polarised world where nobody agrees on everything, and when you look at public opinion, there's a majority of people who agree on legal cannabis." "We've made a ton of progress," he says, "but there's still a long way to go." Please visit BBC Action Line for support with drug addiction. -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn .   Business Drugs Features

2026年3月26日 分享 保存 在Google上添加为首选 迈克·温德林 大麻在该州合法化五年后，在纽约似乎无处不在。但企业主表示，许多合法门店正在苦苦挣扎——主要原因是灰色市场蓬勃发展，以及美国大麻产业复杂的法律地位。如果你最近去过纽约，你很可能注意到了某些现象。杂货店外的广告展示着鲜绿色花朵的图片，类似咖啡馆或电子产品商店的高端药房欢迎来自世界各地的顾客，当然还有那股气味——似乎无处不在，甚至连美国网球公开赛的选手都曾抱怨过。大麻无处不在。从外部看，这像是一场混战，甚至连广泛支持合法化目标（包括减少危害和增加税收）的声音也对此表示怀疑。社交媒体上充斥着抱怨（典型评论包括“纽约不可能把合法大麻搞得更糟了！”），多年来当地媒体一直在记录“大麻杂货店”的兴起——通常是售卖来源可疑产品的街角商店。在全国范围内，大麻消费量有所增加——尽管研究表明，自世纪之交以来，年轻人使用率已逐渐下降。最近事态可能达到了临界点，《纽约时报》——曾经支持合法大麻——发表了一篇题为“大麻无处不在。这是个问题”的社论。该报现在认为“大麻造成的危害超出预期”，并呼吁加强监管。但这股新的绿色浪潮并不像表面看起来那么简单。企业主表示，公众认知已被非法经营者玷污，许多正规企业正在苦苦挣扎——主要原因是美国大麻产业极其复杂的法律地位。“乍一看，纽约的大麻产业似乎正在蓬勃发展，”大麻商人、纽约大麻零售协会运营副总裁杰森·坦塔洛说。“但这种印象最初是由非法经营者的过度饱和所驱动的。“这些店铺往往把自己包装成合法商家，制造出一种误导性的规模感和经济繁荣感，”他说。纽约州五年前的这个时候将娱乐性大麻使用合法化。但法律纠纷和许可证发放缓慢阻碍了初期增长，而加利福尼亚等其他州的销售却在飞速发展。瓶颈如此严格，以至于纽约的一些种植者抱怨他们的作物因缺乏零售销售渠道而白白浪费。与此同时，数百家灰色门店如雨后春笋般涌现，尤其是在

在纽约市，那些疯狂的日子可能即将结束。州政府当局开始打击非法经营者，警方已被授权可以立即关闭无证店铺。与此同时，更多合法企业正在设立，以满足被压抑的需求。“之前确实失控了，”曼哈顿因伍德街区大麻零售商Happy Munkey的联合创始人弗拉德·包蒂斯塔说。“近期的执法行动起到了一定效果，”他说道，“但还有很长的路要走。”研究大麻行业的CRB Monitor公司统计，全州有超过2000个活跃的大麻商业牌照——包括零售商、批发商、种植者及其他类型的大麻公司——另有近5000份申请正在审批中。影响远不止曼哈顿，在这个面积与英格兰相当的全州各地，大麻商店如雨后春笋般涌现。杰森·坦塔洛就是其中一位店主。早在合法化之前，他就已涉足大麻生意。“最初是为了生存，后来逐渐演变为对这个行业的深度专业积累，”他说。他和妻子布丽特妮在纽约州西部郊区社区维克托创办了Flower City Dispensary零售店，该社区人口约1.6万。坦塔洛表示，尽管大麻行业在全州“高度可见且已常态化”，但只有一小部分合法经营者占据了较大的市场份额。“增长确实存在，但受到制约、分布不均，且仍处于稳定过程中，”他说。纽约的成长阵痛只是大麻极其复杂的法律地位的一个缩影，这种复杂性在全国范围内给企业、消费者和公众带来了困惑。围绕该行业的拼凑式法律体系，是大麻从体面走向违禁再回归的漫长而奇特旅程的产物。美国首任总统乔治·华盛顿曾在其庄园种植大麻作物，这是众所周知的事。但随后一波又一波的限制措施接踵而至，最终在1970年出台法律，将大麻列为附表一类毒品——即限制最严格的类别。尽管美国政府发动了禁毒战争，但要求放宽大麻监管的运动始终存在。进入本世纪初期，这一运动逐渐成为主流。根据民调机构盖洛普的数据，2013年美国支持大麻合法化的人数首次突破50%，如今这一比例已上升至超过三分之二。然而，改革并非全面合法化，而是以零敲碎打的方式在州甚至地方层面推进，形成了各州各自为政的碎片化市场。更麻烦的是，根据联邦法律，大麻仍然是非法的——每年仍有数千人因持有大麻及相关犯罪而被逮捕。这种法律上的

##段落
这种拼凑式的局面带来了一些离奇的后果。一个从纽约向西自驾的旅行者会穿过宾夕法尼亚州，那里娱乐用大麻是非法的，然后进入俄亥俄州，那里已在2023年通过公投合法化。如果他们继续沿80号州际公路行驶，最终会到达印第安纳州（大麻非法）、伊利诺伊州（合法）和艾奥瓦州（非法）——如此类推。这本身就够让人困惑的了。但另一个法律漏洞为各种灰色市场和线上生意打开了大门，实际上让全美几乎所有人都能接触到 cannabis。

##段落
2018年的《农业法案》将四氢大麻酚（THC）含量相对较低的大麻（hemp）合法化——THC是让大麻使用者产生兴奋感的化学物质。大麻中含有CBD——一种不会产生THC那种兴奋感但具有一定健康益处的化学物质。随之而来的是CBD的供应过剩。而在实验室里，CBD可以被转化为具有精神活性的THC。

##段落
“创业者可以说，‘这不过是hemp而已’，即便他们生产的是高度致幻的THC形式，”美国大麻与汉麻贸易协会（ATACH）政策与州倡导副总裁克里斯·林赛（Chris Lindsay）说。该协会代表持牌企业。这些产品在网上或那些大麻杂货店出售——即便是在尚未将大麻合法化的州。

##段落
加州大学戴维斯分校经济学家、《合法大麻能否胜出？：大麻经济的残酷现实》一书合著者罗宾·戈德斯坦（Robin Goldstein）估计，仅次于加利福尼亚的第二大大麻市场在得克萨斯州，尽管这个孤星州全面禁止娱乐用大麻。

##段落
像杰森·安布罗西诺（Jason Ambrosino）这样的企业主，已经习惯了应对不断升级的法律复杂性。安布罗西诺是Veterans Holdings的创始人兼首席执行官，这家大麻企业位于纽约州格洛弗斯维尔，距纽约市以北约三小时车程。他是一名在伊拉克受重伤的退伍军人，在发现医用大麻能有效缓解自己的疼痛后进入了这个行业。他说，如今他的法律麻烦包括：相关规定使他无法向邻近州扩张，也无法获得传统融资渠道。

“有一百万种不同的方式可以获得机构资金，但由于联邦法律，你无法为大麻生意拿到其中任何一种，”他说。尽管逆风重重，安布罗西诺还是设法发展了自己的生意，目前雇用了约80人，并且对纽约州合法店铺牌照增加将意味着未来更多销售机会抱有希望。

readings.title: How October 7 changed everything
body: Today, Explained newsletter How October 7 changed everything We still live in the long shadow of Hamas’s brutal 2023 attack — and Israel’s devastating response to it. by Caitlin Dewey Oct 7, 2026, 9:30 PM UTC Gift Israelis visit the Nova music festival memorial site to mark the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023 attacks. Saeed Qaq/Anadolu via Getty Images Caitlin Dewey is a senior writer and editor at Vox, where she helms the Today, Explained newsletter. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . Jewish communities in Israel and around the world are currently marking the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks that killed 1,200 people and triggered the war in Gaza. Memorials for the victims of the attacks have been held at homes , on highways , and at the site of the Nova music festival. In Tel Aviv, a massive art installation at the Trumpeldor beach commemorated both the victims and the 251 hostages taken by Hamas three years ago. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Of those hostages, 166 have since returned alive, and the remains of the last deceased captive were released to Israel in January. But there’s no undoing the national trauma of the October 7 attacks — the deadliest massacre of Jewish people since the Holocaust — or the brutal retaliatory campaign that Israel launched afterward. Those events profoundly changed Israel, Gaza, the broader Middle East, and the United States, and they continue to shape global and domestic politics. So today, we’re taking a look at the very long shadow of the October 7 attacks and Israel’s response to them. Writing about the first anniversary of October 7 two years ago, Vox’s Zack Beauchamp warned that the “horrors” first triggered by the attacks would continue to unfold in tragic and unforeseeable ways . “Events that might seem contained to the Middle East have come to hurt people around the world,” he wrote, “in ways that we may not yet fully understand or even be capable of predicting.” That hurt has undeniably been most acute in the Gaza Strip, where three years of war have reduced entire cities to rubble. Israel’s military campaign has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — most of them civilians — since October 2023. Most of Gaza’s 2 million residents have also been displaced from their homes, crowded into makeshift shelters and refugee camps riddled with hunger and disease. But the consequences of October 7 extended beyond Gaza. Settler violence against Palestinians intensified in the occupied West Bank. And the ensuing conflicts also weakened Iran and changed the balance of power across the Middle East. That’s because Iran had long relied on its allies, like Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon, to project power and deter attacks by its longtime rival, Israel. After October 7, however, Israel significantly weakened both groups, leaving Iran vulnerable and setting the stage for the direct strikes on Iran that Israel and the US began last winter. Both the war in Iran and the continued occupation of Gaza have badly hurt Israel’s international image. Across 36 countries surveyed by Pew last spring, a median of 67 percent of adults viewed Israel negatively. That disapproval has translated into diplomatic shifts, as well: 155 countries — including longtime allies of Israel, such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia — now officially recognize Palestinian statehood, up from 136 before the war. That doesn’t change much on the ground , but it represents a real rebuke to Israel. In the US, meanwhile, Israel has become a huge flashpoint in domestic politics . While more than half of Americans had a favorable view of the country before October 7, sentiment deteriorated sharply in 2025 and 2026, particularly on the left . The issue could help determine some key midterm races, like the Michigan Senate election, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has called for ending US military aid to Israel. That’s a policy nearly half of House Democrats and many potential presidential candidates have also endorsed . What would actually happen if the US cut off aid to Israel? Cutting off US aid to Israel isn’t likely to change the country’s stance toward Palestinians, however. (Israel is a wealthy country in its own right, and American aid represents just a small piece of its budget.) Instead, changing Israeli policy on Gaza and the West Bank would likely require far more aggressive pressure — pressure that, even in the current political environment, the US is unlikely to apply. A single day may have kicked off a cascade of hurt and horrors. But putting an end to them will take far more time. ➨ Cultivate hope. It can feel difficult (not to mention: naive, pointless, and exhausting) to maintain optimism in the face of current events. So Jamil Zaki, a psychology professor and the director of the Stanford Social Neuroscience Lab, suggests another tact: Do away with blind optimism and lean into hope — that belief that the future could turn out well, but requires real care and attention. Did you know… that sea turtles regularly cry (okay: “shed tears”) to rid their bodies of excess salt? Scientists are studying sea turtle tears to learn more about animal navigation. Today’s trivia: What’s the word for a baby eagle? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the final letter of the Greek alphabet. That would be omega, as in the Bible verse, Swiss watch brand, and nutritional supplement . ##段落
Today, Explained 时事通讯：10月7日如何改变了一切。我们至今仍生活在哈马斯2023年残暴袭击——以及以色列对其毁灭性回应——的漫长阴影之下。作者：凯特琳·杜威，2026年10月7日，晚9:30 UTC。

##段落
以色列人参观诺瓦音乐节纪念地，以纪念2023年10月7日袭击三周年。Saeed Qaq/Anadolu via Getty Images。凯特琳·杜威是Vox的高级撰稿人兼编辑，负责主持《Today, Explained》时事通讯。本文发表于《Today, Explained》，这是一份每日时事通讯，帮助你了解当天最引人关注的新闻与故事。点此订阅。

##段落
以色列及世界各地的犹太社区目前正在纪念10月7日袭击三周年。那次袭击造成1200人死亡，并引发了加沙战争。袭击遇难者的纪念活动在住宅、公路以及诺瓦音乐节现场举行。在特拉维夫，特朗普尔德海滩上的一件大型艺术装置同时纪念了遇难者和三年前被哈马斯劫持的251名人质。

##段落

##段落
在这些被劫持的人质中，有166人此后活着返回，最后一名已故被扣押者的遗体也已于今年1月交还以色列。但10月7日袭击——大屠杀以来针对犹太人最致命的屠杀——以及以色列随后发动的残酷报复行动所造成的国家创伤，已无法抹去。这些事件深刻改变了以色列、加沙、更广泛的中东地区以及美国，并持续塑造着全球与各国内部政治。因此今天，我们来审视10月7日袭击及其以色列回应所投下的漫长阴影。

##段落
两年前，在撰写10月7日一周年纪念文章时，Vox的扎克·博尚警告说，最初由这些袭击引发的“恐怖”将以悲剧性且难以预见的方式继续展开。“那些看似局限于中东的事件，已经开始伤害世界各地的人们，”他写道，“其方式或许我们尚未完全理解，甚至可能无法预测。”

##段落
这种伤害无疑在加沙地带最为严重。三年战争已将整座整座城市化为废墟。自2023年10月以来，以色列的军事行动已造成超过7.4万名巴勒斯坦人死亡——其中大多数是平民。加沙200万居民中的大多数也已流离失所，挤在充斥着饥饿与疾病的临时避难所和难民营中。但10月7日的后果并不限于加沙。在被占领的约旦河西岸，定居者对巴勒斯坦人的暴力行为加剧。而随之而来的冲突也……

##段落
伊朗遭到打击，中东力量平衡随之改变。原因在于，伊朗长期依赖其盟友——如加沙的哈马斯和黎巴嫩的真主党——来投射力量并威慑宿敌以色列的攻击。然而10月7日之后，以色列大幅削弱了这两个组织，使伊朗陷入脆弱境地，也为以色列和美国去年冬天开始对伊朗发动直接打击埋下伏笔。伊朗战争与对加沙的持续占领，都严重损害了以色列的国际形象。皮尤去年春天在36个国家进行的调查显示，成年人中对以色列持负面看法的中位比例为67%。这种不满也转化为外交层面的转变：包括英国、加拿大、澳大利亚等以色列长期盟友在内的155个国家，现已正式承认巴勒斯坦建国，而战前这一数字为136。这在实地并未改变太多，但代表着对以色列的切实谴责。与此同时，在美国，以色列已成为国内政治的重大引爆点。10月7日之前，超过半数美国人对以色列持正面看法，但2025年和2026年情绪急剧恶化，尤其是在左翼阵营。这一问题可能影响一些关键中期选举选情，比如密歇根州参议院选举，民主党人阿卜杜勒·埃尔-赛义德已呼吁终止美国对以色列的军事援助。这一政策也已获得近半数众议院民主党人和许多潜在总统候选人的支持。如果美国真的切断对以色列的援助，会发生什么？然而，切断美国对以色列的援助未必会改变该国对巴勒斯坦人的立场。（以色列本身就是一个富裕国家，美国的援助仅占其预算的一小部分。）相反，要改变以色列在加沙和约旦河西岸的政策，可能需要远比这更强硬的施压——而即便在当前政治环境下，美国也不太可能施加这种压力。一天之内，或许就开启了一连串的伤害与恐怖。但要终结这一切，还需要远更多的时间。

##段落
➨ 培育希望。面对当下时事，保持乐观可能很难（更不用说还会显得天真、无意义且令人疲惫）。因此，心理学教授、斯坦福社会神经科学实验室主任贾米尔·扎基建议换一种思路：摒弃盲目乐观，转向希望——即相信未来可能变好，但这需要真正的关切与投入。
